Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be the affine Minkowski model ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), let $c>0$ be the model's positive numerical constant, and let $\Omega\subseteq A$ be a nonempty open set.

(a) A **stress-energy tensor** on $\Omega$ of class $C^k$, $k\ge0$ (with $C^0$ meaning continuous), is a $C^k$ symmetric type-$(2,0)$ tensor field $T$ on $\Omega$ in the sense of [[def-ck-tensor-field-on-minkowski-space]]: at every $p\in\Omega$ the map $T(p):V^*\times V^*\to\mathbb R$ is bilinear and symmetric, so in every inertial chart its components satisfy $T^{ab}=T^{ba}$ ([[thm-sr-tensor-and-current-transformation]]\,(iii)).

(b) In each inertial chart $x$ of the model ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]) define the component families $\varepsilon_x:=T^{00}$, $\pi_x^i:=T^{0i}/c=T^{i0}/c$ and $S_x^{ij}:=T^{ij}$. These are numerical component and scaling conventions involving the fixed positive number $c$; their transformation behaviour is inherited from $T$ and no physical units or measurement interpretation form part of this mathematical definition.

(c) When $k\ge1$, the **four-force density** of $T$ is the $C^{k-1}$ field whose inertial components are $f^b:=\partial_aT^{ab}$, where $\partial_a$ are the coordinate partial derivatives of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]] and the sum over $a$ is the standard contraction of a contravariant index with a coordinate derivative. The components $\partial_aT^{ab}$ transform as a vector, so $f$ is a well-defined vector field on $\Omega$ independent of the inertial chart: under an inertial transition $x'=\Lambda x+a$ the components satisfy $\partial'_aT'^{ab}=\Lambda^b{}_d\,\partial_cT^{cd}$ ([[thm-sr-tensor-and-current-transformation]]\,(iv)), which is exactly the vector transformation law of clause (i) applied to the components $f^b$. For $k\ge1$ one says that $T$ is **locally conserved**, or **balanced**, on $\Omega$ when $f=0$ on $\Omega$, and that $T$ is **balanced against the four-force density** $f$ when $\partial_aT^{ab}=f^b$.

(d) The definition asserts no conservation of any prescribed symmetric field $T$: whether a given $T$ is conserved, whether it arises from an action or a matter model, and whether any of its integrals over a slice converges are separate hypotheses stated elsewhere. No choice principle is used. For a merely continuous tensor ($k=0$) the component conventions and pointwise contractions of (b) are defined, while the divergence, the four-force density and the balance terminology of (c) require the additional $C^1$ hypothesis; no derivative of a merely continuous field is asserted.

I \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $I$ ([[def-continuity-real]]) and differentiable at every point of $I$ that is interior to $I$ ([[def-interior-closure-boundary-r]], [[def-derivative]]), with $$f'(x) = 0 \qquad \text{at every interior point } x \text{ of } I .$$ Then $f$ is constant on $I$: there is a real $k$ with $f(x) = k$ for every $x \in I$.
If the line map $t\mapsto f(a+tv)$ is defined near $0$, its derivative at $0$ is the **directional derivative**

derivations.claim: Components of the coordinate divergence. The components of $T$ are $T^{00}=\rho(x^1)$, $T^{11}=P(x^1)$ and $T^{ab}=0$ for all other pairs; these are $C^1$ in $x$, so the coordinate divergence has components $D^0=\partial_0T^{00}+\partial_1T^{10}=\partial_0\rho(x^1)=0$, $D^1=\partial_0T^{01}+\partial_1T^{11}=P'(x^1)$, and $D^2=D^3=0$, because the omitted terms involve the zero components and $\rho,P$ do not depend on $x^0$.

Vanishing coordinate divergence and constancy of $P$. By construction the set of values $x^1(p)$, $p\in\Omega$, is exactly the interval $J$ on which $\rho,P$ are defined. The set $J$ is open: a chart ball about any point of $x(\Omega)$ permits all sufficiently small changes of its $x^1$ coordinate, hence a neighbourhood of each value in $J$ remains in $J$; this is also true when $J=\varnothing$. Thus every point of $J$ is interior. By step 1.1, $D=0$ on $\Omega$ if and only if $P'=0$ at every interior point of $J$; by [F2] this holds if and only if $P$ is constant on $J$. For nonempty $\Omega$, this is exactly local conservation by [F1]. For $\Omega=J=\varnothing$, $D=0$ and constancy of the empty function $P$ are both vacuous, with any real constant, for example $0$, witnessing constancy. The energy density $\rho$ is subject to no such condition: $\rho'$ never enters the divergence, because the only term containing $\rho$ is $T^{00}$, whose first index is contracted with $\partial_0$ and which is independent of $x^0$.

routine_steps.claim: For nonempty $\Omega$, consequently, a static uniaxial stress in equilibrium has uniform stress $P$ along the stressed direction, while its energy density may vary; when $P<0$ (tension) the tension must be constant. This is a component computation for the stated field; it asserts no material model, no equation of state and no force law.
